newsitem.title: BURMA: Suu Kyi movement suffers as Burma rulers hold firm.
newsitem.headline: Suu Kyi movement suffers as Burma rulers hold firm.

text.p: Aung San Suu Kyi's democracy movement is suffering from intimidation and a lack of well-defined policies, strengthening the position of Burma's military government, analysts said on Tuesday.

Increased intimidation tactics by the ruling State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC) against Suu Kyi's National League for Democracy (NLD) over the past few months have taken a toll on the party and its leaders.

Attendance has dropped at weekend speeches at the front gates of Suu Kyi's lakeside home, with supporters fearing reprisals from the government, as word of arrests and threats of arrests spread among the crowd.
"A lot of it is fear," said a diplomat standing in the rain with a crowd of about 1,500 people during Suu Kyi's speech on Saturday. "The SLORC knows what it's doing and it's working.
"People don't want to get arrested, and they seem to pick out key people in the crowd. Since she's not really able to say much new they don't think it's worth it to risk coming."
In May and early June, crowds of up to 10,000 chanting supporters gathered to hear Suu Kyi speak at the weekend. The crowds now rarely cheer and the applause is quiet.
Suu Kyi lashed out at the country's military rulers at a news conference on Saturday, saying they were trying to crush the democracy movement by misusing the law.
At least 61 supporters of the NLD have been arrested since May and about 30 had been sentenced to long jail terms, Suu Kyi said, complaining that the charges are often trumped up.
The arrests come after a sweeping crackdown in May when the government arrested over 260 of Suu Kyi's followers ahead of a controversial party meeting.
Suu Kyi also said the military government was not allowing the NLD to function as a legally registered organisation, with party officials regularly being intimidated by the government.

In June the SLORC passed a sweeping law effectively muzzling Suu Kyi. It prohibited any individual or organisation from making comments or distributing literature seen as contrary to the government or its efforts to draft a new constitution.
Since June, Suu Kyi has softened her attacks on the SLORC which often centred on its efforts at writing a constitution.
The NLD, which won a landslide victory in a 1990 election but was never allowed to take power, is now drafting its own charter because it says the SLORC's methods are undemocratic.
The NLD angered the SLORC in November when it pulled out of the national convention, which comprises mostly hand-picked delegates and has been meeting intermittently since 1993.

Some analysts said by pulling out, Suu Kyi closed the only door open for dialogue. Since her release from six years of house arrest in July, 1995, Suu Kyi has called for talks with the military council to try to find a way to bring democracy to Burma.

"There seem to be a lot of gaps in their party policy, which has been evident since November when they pulled out of the convention and basically got rid of any chance they had for talking with the SLORC," said one diplomat.
In a news conference on Saturday, Suu Kyi was not her typical confident self, but seemed flustered and angry and was unable to clearly define party policies on various issues.
"She is upset about the arrests," said one political analyst. "She has lost several key people and they can't seem to formulate policies."

The military government has taken advantage of Suu Kyi's weakness. In a well-organised news conference on Monday the government presented flow charts and maps and officials from various ministries were prepared to answer questions on any subject.
"They were slick," said one diplomat. "I think it's very good they were able to stand up there and take all those questions, even if they didn't answer them all."
The government, which has regularly accused foreign media of biased reporting, recently began holding monthly news conferences for foreign and local journalists.
The SLORC took power in 1988 after quashing democracy demonstrations which left thousands dead or in jail.
